core: A factor of safety is a ratio of a capacity to a demand, and the number is uninterpretable until both terms are named
Three axes of ambiguity in a quoted factor: on yield versus on ultimate, applied to load versus to stress, design factor versus realized factor
Margin of safety as a normalised restatement of the same ratio
What the factor covers: uncertainty in loads, material property scatter, analysis idealisation, manufacturing variation, service degradation
What the factor does not cover: an unconsidered failure mode, or ignorance a designer could have removed by analysis or test
Allowable stress design versus load and resistance factor design, and why partial factors on loads and resistances track uncertainty better than one global multiplier
Reliability-based design at concept level: limit states, the reliability index beta, p_f = Phi(-beta), and the notional-probability caveat
Failure modes with the condition that provokes each: yielding, ductile rupture, brittle fracture, fatigue, creep, buckling, wear, corrosion, thermal
Fatigue specifics: S-N behaviour, the endurance limit and its material and environment dependence, the dominant role of stress concentration and surface finish, lifetime scatter
Buckling as a stability failure rather than a strength failure, decided by slenderness, with yield strength absent from the elastic critical load
Static failure theories at survey level: maximum shear stress (Tresca) and distortion energy (von Mises) for ductile behaviour, maximum normal stress (Rankine) where fracture precedes yield
Systems view: single-point failure, redundancy and its independence requirement, fail-safe versus fail-secure, damage tolerance versus safe-life, FMEA
supporting: Limit load and ultimate load as defined for transport-category airplanes, and the two-tier strength and deformation check in 14 CFR 25.305
Scatter factor as a life-reduction divisor applied to fatigue test results
Critical slenderness ratio beta_c = pi*sqrt(E/sigma_y) as the boundary between elastic buckling and yielding
Nil-ductility transition temperature as the reason a fracture mode can switch with temperature
Homologous-temperature thresholds at which creep becomes relevant (0.3 T_m metals, 0.5 T_m ceramics)
Why an integer design factor and the realized factor differ once stock sizes are chosen
Corrosion fatigue and fretting as combined chemical-mechanical degradation modes

Property categories, hardness and impact test methods, and handbook versus design values (owned by engineering-fundamentals:materials:material-properties)

Test method design, instrumentation, verification versus validation and measurement uncertainty (owned by engineering-fundamentals:engineering-practice:testing-and-validation)
Professional conduct, licensure duties, and the obligation to report unsafe conditions (owned by engineering-fundamentals:engineering-practice:engineering-ethics)

claims.claim: Federal airworthiness regulation for transport-category airplanes specifies strength requirements in terms of limit loads, defined as the maximum loads to be expected in service, and ultimate loads, defined as limit loads multiplied by prescribed factors of safety; unless otherwise provided, prescribed loads are limit loads.

Unless otherwise specified, 14 CFR 25.303 requires a factor of safety of 1.5 to be applied to the prescribed limit loads considered as external loads on the structure, and no further factor need be applied where a loading condition is already prescribed in ultimate-load terms. The factor is applied to load, not to stress.

14 CFR 25.305 imposes a two-tier check against two different capacities: the structure must support limit loads without detrimental permanent deformation, and must support ultimate loads without failure for at least three seconds. A single quoted factor therefore hides two distinct governing conditions.

NASA-STD-5001B defines factors of safety as multiplying factors applied to limit loads or stresses, for analytical assessment (design factors) or test verification (test factors), and defines margin of safety as the allowable load, yield or ultimate, divided by the product of limit load and the corresponding yield or ultimate factor of safety, minus one; the standard notes explicitly that 'load' may refer to force, stress, or strain.

The required structural factor is not a property of the physical problem but of the verification approach and the governing document: NASA-STD-5001B tabulates separate yield and ultimate design factors that depend on whether the structure is prototype-tested, protoflight-tested or accepted by analysis alone, and states that increasing the design factors of safety does not by itself justify a no-test approach.

Allowable stress or working stress design computes elastic stresses under service loads and requires them to stay below allowable stresses set as a preset fraction of yield strength, crushing strength or modulus of rupture; those fractions were set empirically to reflect the profession's feeling about the relative variability of materials.

A single set of allowable stresses cannot deliver a constant level of safety. Two roofs designed for the same snow load to the same allowable stresses have different failure probabilities if their dead-to-live load ratios differ, because dead load can be estimated with much more precision than snow load; the working-stress format can also be unsafe when one load counteracts another, a mechanism to which the failure of the Ferrybridge cooling towers has been attributed.

Load and resistance factor design applies partial factors in the form phi*R_n >= sum(gamma_i * Q_i), where R_n is a nominal resistance corresponding to a stated limit state, phi is a resistance factor less than unity reflecting uncertainty in the resistance, and each load effect Q_i carries its own factor gamma_i generally larger than unity reflecting the uncertainty in that load.

The NBS SP 577 study derived the load combinations 1.4D; 1.2D + 1.6L; 1.2D + 1.6S + (0.5L or 0.8W); 1.2D + 1.3W + 0.5L; 1.2D + 1.5E + (0.5L or 0.2S); and 0.9D - (1.3W or 1.5E). Applied to two members carrying the same 100 kN service total, one with 80 kN dead and 20 kN live and one with 20 kN dead and 80 kN live, the 1.2D + 1.6L combination demands 128.0 kN and 152.0 kN respectively, 18.8 percent more capacity of the live-dominated member, while a single service-load ratio cannot distinguish them. Arithmetic executed in Python.

In probability-based limit states design, resistance R and load effect Q are treated as random variables, failure is the event R - Q < 0, and the reliability index beta relates to the probability of failure by p_f = Phi(-beta). Where the probability laws cannot be determined exactly, the resulting p_f is explicitly a notional probability to be interpreted comparatively rather than in a classical relative-frequency sense. The SP 577 study adopted target values of beta = 3.0 for dead-plus-live and dead-plus-snow combinations, 2.5 for combinations containing wind and 1.75 for those containing earthquake. Evaluated in Python, Phi(-3.0) = 1.350e-3, Phi(-2.5) = 6.210e-3 and Phi(-1.75) = 4.006e-2.

Ultimate limit states in structural codes explicitly include loss of load-bearing capacity by exceeding material strength, buckling, fracture, fatigue or fire, and loss of equilibrium as a rigid body, so buckling sits alongside strength as a distinct limit state rather than inside it.

Yield is driven by shearing stresses sliding one atomic plane along another, while fracture is driven by normal stresses acting to separate one plane from another; brittle materials such as ceramics fracture before they yield, and below a ductile-brittle transition temperature a material will fracture before it yields, a mechanism implicated in ship and pipeline failures during winter temperatures.

For multiaxial stress states, the maximum shear stress (Tresca) criterion holds that yield occurs when the maximum shear stress reaches a critical value k, giving k = sigma_Y/2, while the von Mises criterion takes the driving force to be the strain energy of the deviatoric stress components and gives k = sigma_Y/sqrt(3); von Mises often fits experimental data somewhat better and is routinely computed by commercial finite element codes. With an illustrative sigma_Y of 250 MPa these give 125.000 MPa and 144.338 MPa, a 15.47 percent disagreement, computed in Python.

The Rankine or maximum normal stress criterion predicts failure when the maximum principal (normal) stress reaches the uniaxial strength value; it is the most conservative of the three common loci and, missing shear stress, does not accurately describe ductile yielding. It is the criterion that matches the normal-stress-driven mechanism by which brittle materials fracture before they yield.

Metals that sustain substantial plastic strain before fracturing exhibit ductile fracture; metals that fracture with negligible plastic strain exhibit brittle fracture, which results from cleavage, propagates rapidly, and can occur, where flaws are present, at lower stress levels than a ductile fracture. The temperature above which a material is ductile and below which it is brittle is the nil-ductility transition temperature, which is not precise and varies with prior mechanical and heat treatment and with impurities.

In the presence of a crack the local stresses are modified so severely that an ordinary elastic stress analysis is insufficient, and beyond a critical crack length a crack can propagate catastrophically at a gross stress much less than would normally cause yield or failure in a tensile specimen; the critical stress intensity factor K_Ic is the corresponding measure of material toughness.

Fatigue is damage accumulation under the repetitive application of loads that may be well below the yield point, and is dangerous precisely because a single application of the same load would produce no ill effect, so a conventional stress analysis might lead to an assumption of safety that does not exist; the process is thought to begin at an internal or surface flaw where stresses are concentrated.

On an S-N diagram some materials, notably ferrous alloys, show the curve flattening so that below an endurance limit failure does not occur however long loads are cycled, while other materials such as aluminium show no endurance limit, so the designer must instead keep the planned life short of the S-N curve. Fatigue lifetimes scatter over orders of magnitude at fixed stress amplitude because fatigue measures variability in cycles at a given stress rather than variability in stress at one cycle.

Fatigue substantiation must reflect the real article: test specimens and surface conditions should be representative of the production article, with special attention to areas of stress concentration such as holes, joints, changes in section, sharp corners, and rough surface finish. A scatter factor, a statistically derived life-reduction divisor, is applied to fatigue test results to account for variation in fatigue performance.

An endurance limit measured in laboratory air does not survive a corrosive environment: fracture by corrosion fatigue generally occurs at a stress level far below the fatigue limit in laboratory air even though the corrosion is relatively minor, and no metal is immune to cyclic stressing in a corrosive environment.

Corrosion is the electrochemical deterioration of a metal through reaction with its environment, converting it into a metallic compound such as an oxide, hydroxide or sulfate, and is distinct from erosion, which destroys by mechanical action; fretting is abrasive wear at the interface of two loaded surfaces rubbed together by vibration, and can cause severe pitting. Concealed stress is more critical than design stress because stress-corrosion is difficult to recognise before it has overcome the structure's design safety factor.

Creep is time- and temperature-dependent plastic deformation in crystalline materials that becomes a relevant mechanism in metals above roughly 0.3 of the absolute melting temperature and in ceramics above roughly 0.5, and it is insidious because the stress at which it proceeds is much less than the reported yield stress; it passes through primary (transient), secondary (steady-state) and tertiary (runaway) regimes.

Thermal stresses arise when a material is heated or cooled under constraint, or heated or cooled non-uniformly; a constrained body that cannot expand develops stress as its temperature changes, and such stresses, being cyclic in nature, can themselves lead to fatigue failure.

Stability of an elastic equilibrium is decided by the sign of the second variation of the total potential energy, positive meaning stable, zero neutral and negative unstable. Vanishing of the first variation establishes equilibrium and says nothing about whether that equilibrium is stable, so stability is a separate question from whether a stress has reached a strength value.

For a pin-pin column the critical buckling load is P_c = pi^2*E*I/l^2 and the critical buckling stress is sigma_c = pi^2*E/beta^2, where beta = l/rho is the slenderness ratio and rho is the radius of gyration; setting sigma_c equal to sigma_y gives a critical slenderness beta_c = pi*sqrt(E/sigma_y), above which a column buckles elastically before yielding and below which it yields before buckling. The yield strength does not appear in the elastic critical load at all.

Worked buckling-versus-yielding comparison, executed in Python with units carried and using clearly labelled illustrative properties (sigma_y = 250 MPa, sigma_u = 400 MPa, E = 200 GPa): solid square section h = 40 mm gives A = 1600 mm^2, I = 213333.3 mm^4, rho = 11.5470 mm and beta_c = 88.8577, so L_c = 1026.04 mm. At L = 2000 mm, beta = 173.205 and sigma_c = 65.797 MPa, giving P_cr = 105.276 kN against P_yield = 400.0 kN, so buckling governs by a factor of 3.800. At L = 600 mm, beta = 51.962 and sigma_c = 731.082 MPa, so yielding governs. A strength-only design at a factor of 2 on yield would permit 200.0 kN, which is 1.90 times the 2 m column's collapse load.

Worked two-definition factor arithmetic, executed in Python with units carried and illustrative properties: a 20 mm round bar has A = 314.159 mm^2, so a 60 kN axial load produces sigma = 190.986 MPa; the factor on yield is 1.3090 and the factor on ultimate is 2.0944, a ratio of exactly sigma_u/sigma_y = 1.6000. Designing the same bar to a factor of 2.0 requires A = 480.000 mm^2 (d = 24.7215 mm) on yield but only A = 300.000 mm^2 (d = 19.5441 mm) on ultimate, 60 percent more material for the same stated factor. Rounding the yield-based result up to a 26 mm stock diameter gives A = 530.929 mm^2, sigma = 113.009 MPa and a realized factor of 2.2122 against a design factor of 2.000.

Airworthiness regulation requires an evaluation showing that catastrophic failure due to fatigue, corrosion, manufacturing defects, or accidental damage will be avoided throughout the operational life of the airplane, and requires inspections or other procedures to be established on the basis of that evaluation. Inspection thresholds must be set assuming the structure contains an initial flaw of the maximum probable size that could exist as a result of manufacturing or service-induced damage.

The same rule subordinates safe-life to damage tolerance: compliance with the damage-tolerance requirements is not required only if the applicant establishes that their application to particular structure is impractical, in which case the structure must be shown to withstand the repeated loads expected during its service life without detectable cracks, with appropriate safe-life scatter factors applied. The rule also uses 'fail-safe' as a structural category, naming multiple load path fail-safe structure and crack arrest fail-safe structure alongside single load path structure.

In structural usage, fail-safe is the attribute that permits a structure to retain its required residual strength for a period of unrepaired use after the failure or partial failure of a principal structural element, and is typically achieved by a redundant or multi-load-path design; damage tolerance is the attribute that permits it to retain required residual strength for a period of use after sustaining a given level of fatigue, corrosion, accidental or discrete source damage; and safe-life is the number of events during which there is a low probability that strength will degrade below its design ultimate value due to fatigue cracking.

In the security and computing sense the two terms are opposites rather than synonyms: fail safe is a mode of termination of system functions that prevents damage to specified system resources and entities, including life and property, when a failure occurs, though the failure might still cause a security compromise; fail secure is a mode of termination that prevents loss of secure state when a failure occurs, though the failure might still cause damage to a system resource or entity.

NASA's reliability and maintainability standard defines a single point failure as an independent element of a system, hardware, software, or human, the failure of which would result in loss of objectives, hardware, or crew; defines redundancy as the use of more than one independent means to accomplish a given function, with design redundancy requiring that a failure in one function does not impair the system's ability to transfer to a second; defines a failure mode as the particular way in which a failure can occur, independent of the reason for failure, giving short, open, fracture and excessive wear as examples; and defines FMEA as a bottom-up, systematic, inductive, methodical analysis performed to identify and document all identifiable failure modes at a prescribed level and specify their resultant effects, usually performed to identify critical single failure points in hardware.

conflictingEvidence.issue: There is no single definition of 'factor of safety' across engineering practice.
positions: Aviation regulation applies the factor to load: 14 CFR 25.303 multiplies prescribed limit loads by 1.5 to obtain ultimate loads.
Classical allowable stress design applies the reduction to stress: the allowable stress is a preset fraction of a strength value and the computed elastic stress must stay below it (NBS SP 577).
NASA-STD-5001B keeps yield and ultimate factors as separate quantities, distinguishes design factors from test factors, and normalises the result as a margin of safety.
Limit states codes abandon a single global factor in favour of separate load and resistance factors.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats the plurality as the point rather than picking a winner: it defines the factor generically as capacity over demand, teaches the three axes of ambiguity (yield versus ultimate, load versus stress, design versus realized), and states that a quoted number is uninterpretable until those axes are fixed. No universal value or definition is asserted, and no number is offered as design guidance.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a computed probability of failure is a real probability.
positions: Reliability-based design computes p_f = Phi(-beta) from the limit-state statistics.

NBS SP 577 states that where the probability laws cannot be determined exactly, the resulting p_f is a 'notional' probability that should be interpreted, at best, comparatively rather than in a classical relative-frequency sense.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson introduces beta and p_f conceptually and carries the notional caveat explicitly, so students do not read a code-implied p_f as a predicted collapse frequency. This is also written into Common Mistakes.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The Wierzbicki source's illustrative critical slenderness for a square mild-steel column is rounded.
positions: The source states (l/h)_c = pi*sqrt(E/sigma_y)/(2*sqrt(3)) is approximately 30 for E = 210 GPa and sigma_y = 250 MPa.
Evaluating the same expression in Python gives 26.2844.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson does not reproduce the source's rounded figure. It uses the formula and computes its own illustrative case from scratch (E = 200 GPa, sigma_y = 250 MPa, h = 40 mm), reporting beta_c = 88.8577 and L_c = 1026.04 mm, all executed in Python. The discrepancy is recorded here only so a reviewer comparing the two is not confused.

conflictingEvidence.issue: 'Fail-safe' means two different things in the two literatures this lesson draws on.
positions: In airworthiness structures, fail-safe is the retention of residual strength after a principal structural element fails, achieved by redundant load paths (FAA AC 23-13A; 14 CFR 25.571).
In security and computing, fail safe and fail secure are contrasting termination modes, one protecting life and property and one protecting secure state (NIST CSRC glossary, from CNSSI 4009-2015).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states both senses explicitly and does not blend them, because the fail-safe versus fail-secure contrast only makes sense in the second sense while the redundancy discussion belongs to the first.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted that 'Safety Factors And Failure is a foundational concept in Engineering Fundamentals' and described it as a device for organising information. A factor of safety is a specific computed ratio with several incompatible definitions in circulation, not an organising label.

The draft's claim that the topic is best understood by defining it and applying it to a simple scenario is content-free and unsourced; nothing in the research supports treating the topic as a vocabulary exercise.
The draft's Eli-10 material ('a label on a toolbox drawer', 'reading a map legend') has no relationship to the mechanics of failure and carried no statement of where the analogy breaks down.
The draft implied a single settled meaning for 'safety factor'. Every source consulted shows the term is used with several incompatible meanings, which is the central correction this lesson makes.
The draft contained no failure modes at all, and therefore no coverage of buckling, fatigue, creep, brittle fracture, wear, corrosion, or thermal failure.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft; none of its wording survives.

This topic also had an unfinished, never-validated lesson JSON and evidence packet left by an interrupted earlier worker. Both were overwritten. Every source in the carried-over packet was independently re-fetched and re-read in this run, and every number was recomputed from scratch in Python.

Corrected an unsupported statement in the interrupted draft's evidence packet that the reliability index 'generally falls in the range of about 2 to 8'. NBS SP 577 reports observed beta values spanning roughly 1.5 for some metal tension members to over 7 for certain masonry walls, with many flexural and compression members falling between 2.5 and 3.0, and adopted target values of 3.0, 2.5 and 1.75 for different load combinations. The lesson now states the adopted targets rather than a fabricated range.
Defined the factor of safety as a capacity-over-demand ratio and made the ambiguity of that ratio the spine of the lesson.
Added the load-versus-stress distinction grounded in 14 CFR 25.301 and 25.303, which apply the factor to load rather than to stress.

Added the design-factor-versus-realized-factor distinction, the margin-of-safety formulation from NASA-STD-5001B, and the fact that the required factor depends on the verification approach rather than on the physics.
Added the allowable stress design versus load and resistance factor design contrast with the dead-versus-live variability argument from NBS SP 577, plus a computed two-member illustration.
Added the reliability index and notional probability of failure at concept level, with the notional caveat stated rather than suppressed.
Added the full failure-mode inventory, each entry defined by the condition that provokes it, and put the buckling-is-not-a-strength-failure error into Common Mistakes as briefed.

Added the static failure theories at survey level, with the Tresca and von Mises shear-yield disagreement computed rather than asserted, and the Rankine criterion attached to the normal-stress fracture mechanism rather than presented as a yield rule for ductile metals.

Added the systems view with sourced definitions of single-point failure, redundancy, FMEA, fail-safe structure, damage tolerance and safe-life, and separated the structural sense of fail-safe from the security sense in which fail-safe and fail-secure are opposites.
Executed every number in the lesson, its worked example and its questions in Python with units carried, and labelled every material property as illustrative.
Added explicit educational-material and not-design-guidance statements, and stated that real design factors come from the governing code.
rightsIssues: All LibreTexts pages used carry NonCommercial Creative Commons licences: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for the MIT OpenCourseWare derivatives (Roylance 6.1, 6.4, 6.5; Wierzbicki 8.1, 8.6) and for the Cal Poly Humboldt Mechanics and Science of Materials chapter, and CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 for the Cal Poly Humboldt Mechanical Behavior of Material chapter. All are classified REFERENCE_ONLY and no wording from any of them is reproduced. The CC BY-NC-ND page in particular was used only to confirm facts, since that licence forbids adaptation.

eCFR sections, NBS Special Publication 577, NASA-STD-5001B, NASA-STD-8729.1A, FAA advisory circulars and DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93 are U.S. Government works in the public domain. Even so, the lesson paraphrases rather than quoting, apart from short defined terms of art.

The NIST CSRC glossary entries carry definitions derived from CNSSI 4009-2015 and IETF RFC 4949; because the underlying wording has third-party provenance, both records are classified REFERENCE_ONLY and the lesson paraphrases the distinction rather than reproducing the definitions.

Engineering standards published by ASME, ASTM, AISC, ACI, ISO and IEC are copyrighted and were not consulted. No allowable stress, load factor, resistance factor or design value is stated from any standard that was not read in full text.

The load combinations quoted in the partial-factor illustration were read directly in NBS SP 577, a public-domain 1980 NBS report, are labelled there as derived for a then-proposed revision of ANSI A58.1, and are presented in the lesson as a historical illustration of the partial-factor idea rather than as current design values. The lesson states explicitly that a reader must take current factors from the governing code.

sourceRecords.title: Mechanics of Materials (Roylance), 6.5: Fatigue
sourceRecords.notes: Read live with a browser user agent; the page is numbered 6.5 in LibreTexts, not 6.3. Supports fatigue as damage accumulation under repeated loads well below yield, the danger that a single application produces no ill effect so a conventional stress analysis assumes a safety that does not exist, initiation at an internal or surface flaw where stresses are concentrated, S-N curves, the endurance limit in ferrous alloys and its absence in aluminium, and why fatigue lifetimes scatter over orders of magnitude.

sourceRecords.title: Structural Mechanics (Wierzbicki), 8.1: Prelude to Stability of Elastic Structures
sourceRecords.notes: Read live. Supports the central conceptual claim of the buckling section: that equilibrium and stability are separate questions, that vanishing of the first variation of total potential energy establishes equilibrium and says nothing about stability, and that the sign of the second variation decides stable, neutral or unstable.

sourceRecords.title: Structural Mechanics (Wierzbicki), 8.6: Plastic Buckling of Columns
sourceRecords.notes: Read live. Supports the buckling-versus-yielding comparison: the pin-pin critical load P_c = pi^2*E*I/l^2, the critical stress sigma_c = pi^2*E/beta^2 with beta = l/rho and rho the radius of gyration, the critical slenderness beta_c = pi*sqrt(E/sigma_y), and the rule that columns more slender than beta_c buckle elastically before yielding while stockier ones yield first. The page's illustrative (l/h)_c of about 30 is rounded; the lesson computes its own case instead.

sourceRecords.title: Mechanical Behavior of Material, Chapter 10: Creep, Fracture, and Fatigue
sourceRecords.provider: Engineering LibreTexts (California State Polytechnic University, Humboldt)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live; page tags confirm CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, so it was used only to confirm facts and no wording was adapted. Supports the creep entry: creep as time- and temperature-dependent plastic deformation in crystalline materials, relevant above roughly 0.3 T_m in metals and 0.5 T_m in ceramics, insidious because it proceeds far below the measured yield stress, and passing through primary, secondary and tertiary regimes.

sourceRecords.title: Mechanics and Science of Materials, Chapter 6: Mechanical Behavior of Materials Part II
sourceRecords.provider: Engineering LibreTexts (California State Polytechnic University, Humboldt)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live; page tags confirm CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Used to name the Rankine or maximum normal stress criterion, to confirm it predicts failure when the maximum principal normal stress reaches the uniaxial value, that it is the most conservative of the three loci, and that it does not describe ductile yielding because it omits shear. Also cross-checks the Tresca and von Mises statements taken from Roylance.
